title: Trapping Rain Water: two-pointer tracking left-max and right-max.
shortTitle: Trapping Rain Water: Two-Pointer Left-Max and Right-Max
keyPoints: Water trapped above a bar equals min(leftMax, rightMax) minus the bar height, clamped to zero
Two pointers from both ends with running left-max and right-max give O(n) time and O(1) space
Always process the side with the smaller boundary wall because that side's water is fully determined
The prefix-array approach uses O(n) space; two pointers eliminate those arrays
Use long or BigDecimal when summing trapped amounts to avoid overflow in financial calculations
Empty arrays and single-bar inputs return zero because no dip can form

s1_definition.oneliner: Water over a bar is min(leftMax, rightMax) minus the bar height, and two pointers add it from the shorter side.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Trapping Rain Water** – given an array of bar heights, compute how much water is trapped in dips between bars after rain.
- **Water formula** – the water above any single bar equals the smaller of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right, minus the bar's own height, never less than zero.
- **Two-pointer approach** – a left pointer and a right pointer walk inward from both ends, each tracking the running maximum height on its side.
- **Process the shorter side** – at each step, whichever side has the smaller boundary wall is the side whose trapped water can be safely committed.
- **Complexity** – runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space, improving on the prefix-array method that needs O(n) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India plots Rajesh's daily account balances as a skyline of bars. Dips between tall balance days hold trapped reserve that cannot drain. Two fingers walk inward from both ends, each remembering the tallest wall seen so far on its side, and whichever side is shorter is the side whose trapped reserve can be safely tallied.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Trapping Rain Water takes an array of bar heights and computes the total water trapped in dips between taller bars after rain. The water above any single bar equals the smaller of the tallest wall to its left and the tallest wall to its right, minus that bar's own height. The two-pointer solution walks inward from both ends, tracking a running left maximum and right maximum, and commits trapped water on whichever side currently has the smaller boundary.

The correctness insight is that when the left bar is less than or equal to the right bar, the right side already guarantees a wall at least that tall, so the water over the left bar is bounded purely by the left maximum. That certainty lets you commit the left bar's water immediately without knowing the exact right maximum yet, and the mirror argument holds on the right side.

The two-pointer method gives O(n) time with O(1) space, improving over the prefix-array approach that precomputes leftMax and rightMax arrays in O(n) space. For financial skylines spanning years of daily data, the constant-space version is the practical choice.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, Rajesh's daily balance skyline has dips between higher-balance days that represent idle trapped reserves. The two-pointer method computes that trapped reserve across years of daily data in a single linear pass with no extra arrays, giving the treasury dashboard a fast and memory-efficient analytic.

Remember one sentence: process the side with the smaller boundary wall, because the other side guarantees a wall at least as tall, making the near-side max the true limit on trapped water.
